name: The Test-Case Importer
oneLiner: Bulk-creates ADO test cases from an xlsx of steps — grouping rows, encoding steps, linking to the parent story — and files them into a suite.
lead: Testers draft in a spreadsheet — one row per step, with action and expected result. This agent reads it with `xlsx`, groups rows into test cases by title, and creates each as a structured ADO Test Case work item: steps, priority, `TestedBy` link, and owner all set. It emits a before/after mapping of every row to its new work item ID.
chore: Hand-copying tests from a spreadsheet into ADO is mind-numbing. Per test case: open a blank form, type the title, add each step and expected result one by one, set priority, link it to the story, save — then repeat dozens of times. Slow, and skipped steps or wrong links creep in as attention drifts.
instead: The agent reads the whole spreadsheet at once, groups rows into complete test cases, and creates each fully formed — every step, expected results, priority, `TestedBy` link to the parent story, and owner. It writes before/after mapping spreadsheets tracing each row to its new work item ID, and can add the batch straight into a suite.
whyItMatters: A hundred test cases into ADO in minutes instead of a day means testers spend their time testing, not typing into forms.

howItWorks.step: It reads the xlsx (one row per step) and groups rows sharing a `Title` into a single test case, preserving step order.
howItWorks.explain: The spreadsheet is one-row-per-step, but ADO wants one-work-item-per-test-case, so this **groups by `Title`** using a Map: the first row for a title seeds the test case (capturing `Priority` and `Story ID` once, since those repeat identically down the step rows), and every row for that title appends a step. `{ defval: '' }` forces `sheet_to_json` to emit blank cells as `''` rather than omitting the key, so `row['Action']` is always safe to `.trim()`. Two deliberate defaults keep malformed input from producing broken cases: a missing `Priority` falls back to `P2`, and a blank `Expected Result` becomes the generic assertion `Verify action completes successfully` — a step with no expected result is meaningless in ADO. Rows with an empty `Title` are skipped entirely, so spacer rows don't create phantom cases. Map insertion order preserves the sheet's row order, which is what keeps steps sequential.

howItWorks.step: It creates each Test Case work item with its steps, priority, and a `TestedBy-Reverse` link to its parent story.
howItWorks.explain: Creating an ADO work item is a **JSON-Patch document** — an array of `add` ops, one per field, each keyed by its internal **reference name** (`System.Title`, `Microsoft.VSTS.TCM.Steps`, `Microsoft.VSTS.Common.Priority`), never the friendly label shown in the UI. The steps go in as a single field whose value is the serialized XML from `stepsToXml`, and `parsePriority` converts a `P2`-style string to the numeric 1–4 ADO stores. Both `AssignedTo` and the story link are conditional so a case with no owner or no story ID is still valid. The link uses `path: '/relations/-'` (the `-` appends to the relations array) with `rel: TestedBy-Reverse`: from the **test case's** side, *Reverse* is the direction that reads 'this case tests that story' — using Forward here would link it backwards. The relation's `url` must be a full REST API work-item URL, not just the ID.

howItWorks.step: Steps are serialized into ADO's `Microsoft.VSTS.TCM.Steps` XML format, so they render as a numbered step list like a hand-authored test case.
howItWorks.explain:
The `Microsoft.VSTS.TCM.Steps` field has a peculiar, undocumented-in-practice shape that this reproduces exactly: a `` element wrapping one `` each (`ValidateStep` is what gives a step its verifiable *expected result* column, versus a plain action step), and inside every step **two** `parameterizedString`s — first the action, then the expected result, in that order. The tricky part is the **double encoding**: each step's text is really HTML (`

...

`), but it lives inside XML, so the angle brackets are written as entities (`<`/`>`) — the field stores escaped HTML as text. That's also why the user's own text is run through `escapeXml` first: an unescaped `<` or `&` in an action would corrupt the surrounding XML. The `id="0" last="N"` header and per-step `id` are the numbering ADO renders as the step list.

howItWorks.step: It writes a second 'with IDs' xlsx stamping each created test case's new work item ID and URL onto every original step row.
howItWorks.explain: This is the audit trail. It **un-groups** the created cases back to the original one-row-per-step shape — the inverse of the load step — so every input row reappears, now stamped with the `adoId` and `adoUrl` of the work item it became, giving a row-level trace from spreadsheet to live test case. `result.adoId || undefined` matters: a failed creation leaves `adoId` empty, and coercing it to `undefined` makes `json_to_sheet` emit a blank cell rather than a misleading `null` or `0`, so failed rows are visibly un-stamped. The output filename carries `getTimestamp()` so re-runs never overwrite a prior mapping — each import keeps its own dated receipt.

howItWorks.step: If a plan and suite are given, it adds the whole created batch to that suite in one call.
howItWorks.explain: Filing into a suite is **opt-in and separate from creation** — a test case exists in the project the moment it's created; adding it to a suite is a distinct ADO operation, so this whole block is guarded on `planId`, `suiteId`, and `createdIds.length > 0` all being present. Only the *successfully* created IDs (`createdIds`) are passed, so a case that failed to create is never filed. It hands the whole batch to `addTestCasesToSuite` in one call rather than looping, and `configId || undefined` lets ADO fall back to the suite's default test configuration when none was specified rather than sending an empty value.

examples.caption: Import a batch of drafted test cases
examples.input: An xlsx with 3 test cases across 11 step rows, for the 'Search Filters' feature.
examples.output: Created 3 Test Cases: #512, #513, #514 — each with steps, `TestedBy` link, and author as owner. Wrote a mapping stamping every row with its new work item ID.

examples.caption: Preview with --dry-run
examples.output: Would create 3 test cases (11 steps). Listed each title, step count, and parent story — nothing written to ADO.

examples.caption: Import and add to a suite
examples.input: Import the xlsx and add the new test cases to the 'Sprint 7 Regression' suite.
examples.output: Created 3 test cases and added all 3 to the 'Sprint 7 Regression' suite in one run.

underHood.heading: Parsing the xlsx
underHood.whenRuns: First, when you point it at the Excel file.
underHood.input: An xlsx, one row per step.
underHood.output: Test cases grouped by `Title`, each with its ordered step list.

underHood.heading: Writing the 'before' mapping
underHood.whenRuns: Right after parsing, before any work item is created.
underHood.output: A mapping xlsx showing every test case exactly as it's about to be created.

underHood.heading: Creating each Test Case
underHood.whenRuns: Once per test case, in order.
underHood.input: A test case's title, steps, priority, and parent story ID.
underHood.output: A new Test Case work item, steps encoded in the `Microsoft.VSTS.TCM.Steps` XML format.

underHood.heading: Writing the 'with IDs' mapping
underHood.whenRuns: After every test case has been attempted.
underHood.input: Each test case's creation result, success or failure.
underHood.output: A second 'with IDs' xlsx mapping every original row to its new work item ID and URL.

underHood.heading: Adding to a suite (optional)
underHood.input: The list of newly created test case IDs.
underHood.output: The new test cases appear in that suite in ADO.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
Azure DevOps Test Plans access and a **PAT** scoped to create test cases.
An xlsx of drafted tests: one row per step, columns Title, Step #, Action, Expected Result, Priority, and Story ID.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the engine that runs the agent.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is TypeScript run under Node — a one-time per-machine install.

steps.label: Clone the agent and install its dependencies.
steps.why: `npm install` pulls the `xlsx` reader and ADO client into `node_modules`.
steps.firstRun: Cold install — a minute or two.

steps.label: Set the target org, project, and PAT (env vars).
steps.cmd:
export ADO_ORGANIZATION=my-org
export ADO_PROJECT="My Project"
export ADO_PAT=your-access-token
steps.why: Read at startup: which ADO org/project to create the test cases in and the PAT that authorizes it.

steps.label: Preview the grouping with --dry-run.
steps.why: `--dry-run` groups rows into test cases and lists each one's title, step count, and parent story — nothing written to ADO. Verify the grouping before committing.

steps.label: Create the test cases, optionally adding them to a suite.
steps.why: Same grouping, but now each test case is created in ADO — steps, priority, and `TestedBy` link in place — and, because `--plan-id`/`--suite-id` were given, added to that suite in the same run.
steps.rerun: Non-idempotent — re-running the same xlsx creates a duplicate batch. Re-run only on a fresh or updated spreadsheet.

steps.label: Open the before/after mapping workbooks.
steps.why: Both land next to your input file. The first is a snapshot of what was about to be created; the second stamps the real work item ID and URL onto every row, so any step traces back to what it became.

inputs.name: --input <xlsx>
inputs.desc: xlsx with Title, Step #, Action, Expected Result, Priority, and Story ID columns — one row per step.

inputs.name: --plan-id <id> --suite-id <id>
inputs.desc: Optional: add the newly created test cases to this suite.

inputs.name: --stories <ids>
inputs.desc: Optional: only create the test cases belonging to these parent stories.

inputs.name: --dry-run
inputs.desc: Preview the grouped test cases without creating anything.

outputs.name: ADO_Steps_Mapping_<timestamp>.xlsx
outputs.desc: A 'before' snapshot of every test case about to be created, saved next to the input file.

outputs.name: ADO_Steps_Mapping_WithIDs_<timestamp>.xlsx
outputs.desc: The same rows, now stamped with each test case's new work item ID and URL.

outputs.name: new test cases in ADO
outputs.desc: Each fully built — steps, priority, and a `TestedBy` link to its parent story.

runbook.rerun: Non-idempotent — every run creates brand-new work items, so re-running an unchanged xlsx duplicates the batch. Re-run only after editing the spreadsheet, and use `--stories` to scope a re-run to just the changed rows.
runbook.integrate: Hand testers the before/after mapping as a receipt — the `WithIDs` file is the audit trail proving which drafted row became which live test case, and it's the natural input to the results-poster once those cases are executed.

video.caption: A 3-minute screen recording: import a batch of drafted test cases from an xlsx.
script: Open a terminal beside the drafted-tests spreadsheet.
Say: 'This turns a spreadsheet of test steps into real checklists in the tracker.'
Show the spreadsheet — point out the Title, Step #, Action, Expected Result, and Story ID columns.
Run `node -v` and `npm install` (or note it's already done).
Show the `export ADO_...` lines — the only project-specific part.
Run the `--dry-run` command; read out the grouped tests it lists — titles, step counts, parent stories.
Run the same command without `--dry-run` and with `--plan-id`/`--suite-id`; narrate each test being created.
Open the `WithIDs` spreadsheet it produced; show the new tracker ID next to each row.
Switch to the browser tracker and open one of the new checklists — show its steps rendered as a numbered list.
Close: 'That's a day of typing turned into one command.'
